At the gram panchayat office in Yavatmal district, Tejas slapped the yield register on the table. "Look. The six villages that got solar pumps last year harvested far more cotton. The pumps did it."
Vinita, the block's agriculture officer, turned the pages slowly. "Maybe. But which villages got pumps first?"
"The ones that applied fast."
"The ones whose sarpanches know the paperwork, where farmers already had some money. They might have done better anyway. Or did the farmers who were already doing well put in extra for the pumps?" She tapped the rainfall column. "And the eastern side got more rain this year. That's where most pumps are."
Tejas frowned. "So the pumps did nothing?"
"I didn't say that. Find me six similar villages without pumps, same rain, same size farms, and we compare. Then we'll know what to tell the collector."

qa.q: What does the yield register show, according to Tejas?
qa.a: The six villages that got solar pumps last year harvested far more cotton.

qa.q: What is Vinita thinking when she asks which villages got pumps first?
qa.a: She suspects those villages were different to begin with, with better paperwork and more money, so their good harvest might not be the pumps' doing.

qa.q: What comparison does Vinita ask for, and why does it help?
qa.a: Six similar villages without pumps, with the same rain and farm size; comparing them separates the pumps' effect from rain and money.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel when Vinita questions the finding?
qa.a: Tejas might feel the good news is being brushed aside at first, though Vinita makes clear she isn't saying the pumps did nothing.

grounding: It shows an officer asking about third causes, reverse direction and rainfall, and asking for a comparison group before crediting the pumps.

"Customers with the loyalty app spend forty percent more," Kofi announced, pointing at the chart on the big screen in the Rotterdam office. "Let's push the app harder and watch sales climb."
Santiago leaned back. "Or the people who already spend a lot are exactly the ones who bother to download it. That runs the arrow the other way."
"Hm."
"And most of these downloads came in December. Everyone spends more in December." He scrolled. "Also, app users live closer to our shops. Distance could drive both."
Kofi crossed his arms. "So what would convince you?"
"Send the app invite to a random half of new customers next month, and not to the other half. If the invited half spend more, I'm on your side."
Kofi sighed, then grinned. "Fine. Random half it is."

qa.a: Customers with the loyalty app spend forty percent more.

qa.a: He suspects big spenders are simply the ones who download it, that December inflated spending, and that living near the shops could drive both.

qa.q: What test does Santiago propose, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Invite a random half of new customers and not the other half; since chance decides who gets the invite, a spending gap would point to the app itself. 👍

qa.q: What would change if the invited half spent no more than the others?
qa.a: The team would learn the link came from who downloads the app, not from the app, and could stop spending effort pushing it.

Mentor's note, Monday after the Diwali break.
Kamal came to our weekly check-in still rattled. At a family dinner, two uncles and his cousin spoke strongly in favour of the new expressway through the wetland near their town. Kamal said he "couldn't believe" anyone reasonable supported it. He told me, "Literally everyone I know thinks it's a disaster." When I asked who "everyone" was, he listed his environment club, his flatmates and the people he follows online. He paused after that. He admitted his uncles drive trucks on that route every week and had reasons he hadn't heard before. He was still upset, and I didn't try to change his view. We agreed he'd phone one uncle and ask him to explain the road from his side, and just listen.
Rukmini

qa.a: It lets Kamal hear reasons from someone outside his usual circle without turning it into another argument.

qa.a: They might have felt judged by a younger relative who assumed their view was unreasonable, when for them the road is part of their weekly work.

Sunday, late
Still annoyed. At Tarun's engagement lunch someone brought up the firecracker ban for Diwali, and I said, "Obviously it should be banned, everyone agrees on that now." The table went silent. Then Tarun's father said it's their family tradition, and they buy from a small shop in Sivakasi that feeds a whole street. Tarun's grandmother said the children wait all year for it. Maybe my "everyone" is just forty people who think exactly like me. That's an uncomfortable thought.
- Nilesh
